title: Arms transfers, informal economies and firm-reported corruption

sources.name: Informal Economy Database
sources.license: CC BY 4.0 with World Bank dataset terms; attribution retained; selected World Bank model and enterprise-survey tables only
notes: Elgin, C., M. A. Kose, F. Ohnsorge, and S. Yu. 2021. Understanding Informality. CEPR Discussion Paper 16497, Centre for Economic Policy Research, London.
Normalized selected worksheets into country/year observations; numerical units and missing cells retained.
The World Bank reproducibility package also identifies the Informal Economy Database as CC BY 4.0: https://reproducibility.worldbank.org/index.php/catalog/330/download/1002/README.pdf
Workbook period is 1990–2020. Model estimates are not measured criminal-market output. Survey coverage is sparse.
Labor, pension and World Values Survey tables are not redistributed by this collector.

sources.license: CC BY 4.0 with World Bank dataset terms
notes: Country and aggregate classifications bind the geography level of WDI observations. No economic measurements are drawn from this response.

indicators.label: Informal output — DGE model
indicators.description: World Bank Informal Economy Database, DGE_p; original workbook units retained.
limitations: Informality includes lawful unregistered activity; this is not the size of illegal or organized-crime markets.
The retained workbook ends in 2020; retrieval does not make these historical observations current.
DGE and MIMIC are alternative model estimates, not independent measured totals or uncertainty bounds.

limitations: Informality includes lawful unregistered activity; this is not the size of illegal or organized-crime markets.

DGE and MIMIC are alternative model estimates, not independent measured totals or uncertainty bounds.

indicators.label: Major conventional arms imports
indicators.description: Volume of major conventional-weapons transfers through sales, gifts, aid and manufacturing licences, compiled by SIPRI and distributed in World Development Indicators.
limitations: TIV is a transfer-volume measure, not US dollars, a sale price, revenue or illegal-market value; do not divide it by GDP.
These observations do not classify transfers as legal or illegal. Most small arms, light weapons, ammunition and support services are excluded.
A reported zero denotes deliveries between 0 and 0.5 million TIV; it is not proof of no transfers. Null is unavailable.
Country and regional/world totals overlap. SIPRI includes some transfers involving rebel groups; these national aggregates do not resolve individual actors or routes.

indicators.label: Major conventional arms exports
indicators.description: Volume of major conventional-weapons transfers through sales, gifts, aid and manufacturing licences, compiled by SIPRI and distributed in World Development Indicators.
limitations: TIV is a transfer-volume measure, not US dollars, a sale price, revenue or illegal-market value; do not divide it by GDP.
These observations do not classify transfers as legal or illegal. Most small arms, light weapons, ammunition and support services are excluded.
A reported zero denotes deliveries between 0 and 0.5 million TIV; it is not proof of no transfers. Null is unavailable.
Country and regional/world totals overlap. SIPRI includes some transfers involving rebel groups; these national aggregates do not resolve individual actors or routes.

indicators.label: Informal payments to public officials
indicators.description: Share of surveyed establishments considering that similar firms make informal payments or give gifts to public officials to get things done.
limitations: This survey perception measure is not a count of bribes, all corruption, or the value of a black economy.
Survey years are sparse; early survey instruments may differ from the later global methodology. Do not interpolate absent years.
Enterprise Surveys primarily sample formal private firms with at least five workers, not the whole informal economy.

limitations: Informal economic activity includes lawful work and commerce. These indicators do not estimate the size of the drugs, arms or organized-crime markets.
DGE and MIMIC provide alternative model estimates; they are not independent observations to add together.
The informal-output workbook ends in 2020. WDI arms and firm-survey series have their own reported periods. Empty cells remain unavailable; sparse survey years are not interpolated.
UNODC firearms, economic-crime and illicit-financial-flow workbooks were acquired for private research; their quantities remain excluded while source-specific redistribution terms are unresolved.
Legal arms transfers and military spending are not used as estimates of illicit weapons markets.
